newsitem.title: INDIA: India looks beyond Pakistan to greater world role.
newsitem.headline: India looks beyond Pakistan to greater world role.

text.p: India has stepped up its drive to assume greater global influence, staking a claim to a seat on the U.N. Security Council and smoothing over long-festering differences with rival Pakistan, analysts said on Sunday.
India's desire to play a more forceful leadership role was on display last week during a visit by Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral to the United States, they said.

Gujral told the United Nations General Assembly that India deserved a seat on the powerful Security Council, citing its "unwavering commitment" to the U.N., multilateralism and international peace-keeping efforts.
India's claim to the two-year Asian seat on the 15-nation council, to be vacated by Indonesia at the end of the year, put Delhi at odds with Japan, which is also vying for the position.

But India, which has also staked a claim to a permanent seat on an expanded Security Council, seems to have developed a sureness that has encouraged it to contain tension with neighbouring Pakistan, analysts and diplomats said.
For decades, India and Pakistan have used the U.N. podium to wage diplomatic war against each other.

On Thursday, Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto called recent local elections in India's Jammu and Kashmir state a "sham" and proposed an international conference to resolve their long-standing dispute over the Kashmir region.
Turning a deaf ear to Bhutto, Gujral made no mention of Pakistan in his speech to the General Assembly on Friday.

"The rest of the world is irritated by the constant slanging match between India and Pakistan when they meet in multilateral assemblies," former Indian foreign secretary J.N. Dixit told Reuters. "The rest of the world is not interested unless the problems blow up into a major regional crisis."
The studied silence partly reflected India's view that there is little international support for Pakistan's repeated calls for an international conference on Kashmir, analysts said.
Gujral dismissed the proposal as "irrelevant."

The Press Trust of India quoted U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns as reiterating Washington's view that India and Pakistan should solve the Kashmir dispute, which dates to the partition of British India in 1947, in bilateral talks.
Dixit said Pakistan made the same proposal in 1991 and mustered no global support. "It's a non-starter," he said.

Indian foreign policy analysts said Bhutto appeared to be trying to deflect attention from troubles at home, including sectarian strife. "She has her own domestic compulsions," a diplomat in New Delhi said.
Gujral's resounding silence over Pakistan also reflected India's desire to move beyond bilateral tensions with Islamabad that have wound a diplomatic straitjacket around New Delhi.

"We do not want to enter into acrimonious polemics with Pakistan but build people-to-people relations," Gujral told reporters in New York, saying India had eased visa restrictions for Pakistanis and allowed journalists to enter India.
The Hindu newspaper cited the "possibility of a new trend in India's foreign policy -- a shift away from Pakistan-fixation."
Dixit said India felt strengthened by the recently concluded elections in troubled Jammu and Kashmir state and the economic reforms that have attracted foreign investors.
"These have given a certain sense of confidence," he said.

Although India was among a small minority of nations opposed to a global nuclear test ban treaty, Delhi felt it had strengthened its claim to represent the developing world by standing up for total disarmament, officials said.
"India's pitch to developing countries is that if they want an independent voice in the Security Council, capable of an independent line, they should vote for it," the United News of India said.
A U.S. pledge not to allow differences over the nuclear test ban treaty to damage growing bilateral economic and political ties has also emboldened India, Dixit said.
"This lends a certain confidence to India. It makes us look at things in a more rational perspective rather than get emotional," he said.
